title: India Just Reopened All Three Himalayan Trade Routes With China. The Last Caravan Crossed Seven Years Ago.
excerpt: Lipulekh, Shipki La, and Nathu La are all active again for the first time since the Galwan clash. Traders no longer need mules. The Kailash Mansarovar Yatra is back. And for the first time ever, transactions will be in rupees and yuan, not barter.
body:
The first batch of 26 Indian traders — 17 merchants and nine assistants — is expected to cross into Tibet through the Lipulekh Pass in Uttarakhand’s Pithoragarh district this week, marking the resumption of India-China border trade through the pass after a gap of six to seven years. It is the final piece in a quiet but significant reopening: all three traditional Himalayan trade corridors between India and China are now active for the first time since the deadly 2020 Galwan Valley clash shattered relations between the two nuclear powers.

Shipki La in Himachal Pradesh’s Kinnaur district opened on June 1 for a six-month season running through November. Nathu La in Sikkim has been reactivated for the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, with the first batch of ten pilgrim groups departing Delhi on June 15. And Lipulekh, the oldest and most historically charged of the three, is now processing trade passes.

## From Yaks to Trucks

For centuries, trade on these routes meant days of trekking through blizzard-prone passes at 17,000 feet, with goods strapped to yaks, mules, and human backs. The Bhotia and Rung communities of Uttarakhand’s Byans, Darma, and Chaudas valleys built their livelihoods around these caravans, carrying rice, cloth, and spices to Taklakot in Tibet and returning with salt, borax, and wool.

This time, it will be different. A motorable road now reaches to within 200 metres of the Lipulekh Pass — roughly 100 kilometres of tarmac that replaces what used to be a multi-day mountain trek. On the Chinese side, roads connect to Taklakot market, 18 kilometres from the border. For the first time, trucks will carry what mules once did.

The administrative machinery has caught up too. A customs office and a bank branch have been set up at Gunji. A Trade Pass Office was inaugurated in Dharchula, where 103 traders have already applied. A second batch of 25 passes is being processed. At Shipki La, the Kinnaur administration has completed customs workshops, security coordination between the Indian Army, ITBP, and the Customs Department, and trader registration through the Tehsildar at Pooh.

## Rupees and Yuan, Not Barter

Perhaps the most consequential change is invisible. Under a bilateral agreement reached during Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi’s visit to India in August 2025, cross-border trade will for the first time be conducted in rupees and yuan rather than the barter system that has governed these corridors since they reopened in 1991.

The shift from “one nali of rice for five nalis of salt” to currency-based transactions may sound technical, but it effectively transforms what was a subsistence-level cultural exchange into something with the potential to scale. In 2019, the last year the Lipulekh route was active, trade through the pass was worth roughly ₹3 crore — modest, but conducted entirely through barter and human porterage. With roads and currency, the ceiling is dramatically higher.

## The Kailash Mansarovar Yatra Returns

The pilgrimage route has been closed since 2020 — first for COVID, then for the border standoff. Ten batches of pilgrims will undertake the 21-day journey via Nathu La between June and August, with the first group crossing into Tibet on June 20. Each pilgrim pays approximately ₹2.83 lakh. The Sikkim government has built two acclimatisation centres between Gangtok and Nathu La, along with rest houses and facilities along the route.

For millions of Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist devotees across the diaspora, the Yatra’s resumption is more than a logistics story — it is the restoration of access to one of the most sacred sites in their spiritual tradition.

## The Diplomatic Signal

The reopening of all three corridors is being read in diplomatic circles as the most tangible proof yet of the India-China thaw that began with the October 2024 disengagement pact and accelerated through the 24th and 25th rounds of Special Representatives talks. The 35th meeting of the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs, held in Beijing in May, specifically discussed cross-border cooperation, trans-border rivers, and the Yatra.

But the normalisation is selective. India has not reversed its bans on Chinese mobile applications, has maintained extra vetting layers on Chinese investments, and has not restored direct air links. The trade corridors are an olive branch, not a reset — a calculated signal that engagement can proceed on specific, bounded tracks even as the broader strategic competition continues.

Nepal, meanwhile, has renewed its objections to the Lipulekh route, reiterating its claim over the Kalapani-Lipulekh-Limpiyadhura region. India considers the area its own under the 1816 Sugauli Treaty, but the dispute adds a layer of sensitivity to what is already one of the most geopolitically charged trade corridors on the planet.

nri_angle: The Kailash Mansarovar Yatra’s return restores access to one of the most sacred pilgrimage sites for millions of Hindus, Jains, and Buddhists in the diaspora, while the trade reopening signals an India-China normalisation that could reshape investment and travel calculus for NRIs.
